title: Solo Hiking the Lost Lakes Loop (5 Miles Off-Trail)
creator: Wren Halvorsen
description:
14.2 miles, ~4,000 ft of gain, and a cross-country section over a granite saddle. Go after snowmelt, before the late-summer storms, and only if you're comfortable route finding.

Gear: 3L water, filter, puffy, rain shell, first aid, PLB.

Always leave your route and turnaround time with someone.

sentences.t: Morning from the trailhead, it's five forty-five, and it is very cold.
Today I'm hiking the Lost Lakes Loop, about fourteen miles, and the middle section has no trail at all, it's a cross-country route over a granite saddle.
I've wanted to do this one for two years, and the snow finally melted out last week.
Pack check, three liters of water, a filter, lunch, a puffy, a rain shell, a first aid kit, and an emergency beacon.
I'm going solo, so I left my route and my turnaround time with my sister.
Turnaround time is two p.m., no matter where I am.
The first four miles are on a real trail, switchbacks up through the pines.
Not much to say about this part, except that my legs hate me.
Okay, mile four, Upper Lake, and this is where the trail ends.
From here I'm navigating with Trailpath, and they're sponsoring this part of the video, so thanks to them for that.
Last night at home, I drew the route on the map, and it snapped my line to the contours so I could see exactly how steep each section is.
And I downloaded the whole area for offline, because there's zero cell signal up here.
So right now my phone's in airplane mode, and the blue dot still knows exactly where I am.
The plan is to contour around the east side of the lake and then head up this gully to the saddle.
On the map the gully looks fine, but I'm turning on the slope-angle layer, and you can see the top fifty feet go red, which means it's over thirty-five degrees.
So instead I'm going to take the ridge just to the left, it's longer, but it stays orange the whole way.
Okay, I'm up on the ridge now, and I've drifted a bit, the dot says I'm about a hundred feet below my line.
That's the nice thing about having the line drawn, I can see I need to cut up and right before these cliffs.
And here's the saddle, eleven thousand two hundred feet, right on time.
Going down the other side, it's all talus, these big loose boulders, and it's really easy to lose track of where you're heading.
I'm checking the map every few minutes, and I can see the next lake below me, so I just aim for its outlet stream.
Heading down the drainage, I tap the screen and drop a waypoint at this little spring, so I remember there's water here next time.
And there's the trail again, right where the map said it would be, which after five miles of boulders is a beautiful sight.
So, the hard part's done, and it's only twelve thirty.
I'm sitting by Lost Lake number three with my shoes off, and the water is so cold it actually hurts.
There's a family of marmots on the rock behind me who are very interested in my lunch.
No, you can't have it.
The last five miles back are all downhill on a good trail, past three more lakes, each one a slightly different shade of blue.
If you want to do this loop, I really recommend going after the snow melts and before the late summer thunderstorms.
And please don't do the off-trail section unless you're comfortable with route finding, because it's not marked, and there's nobody up there to help you.
I made it back to the car at four fifteen, fourteen point two miles and about four thousand feet of climbing.
Tired, sunburned, and very happy.
Thanks for coming along, and I'll see you on the next one.
